title: Reasons for Action: Internal vs. External

summaries.example: Imagine choosing between two places to eat. One place has your favorite food, so that gives you a reason to go there. The other place is hard to reach, so that gives you a reason not to go. The philosophers in this debate ask: must a reason connect to what a person wants or could be moved to do?
summaries.summary: This topic asks what makes something a reason for action. A reason is a consideration that counts for or against doing something. A motivating reason explains why someone acted, while a normative reason tells us what counts in favor of an action. Reasons internalism says that normative reasons must connect with a person’s motivation or with a motivational state, such as a desire, emotion, intention, or aversion. Some versions say the person must actually be motivated; others say the person would be motivated under special conditions, such as having better information. Reasons externalism rejects the claim that every reason must have this kind of connection. The debate matters because some reasons seem personal and desire-based, while other reasons—especially moral or long-term reasons—seem to apply even when a person lacks the matching desire.
key_ideas: A reason for action is not always the same as the reason that explains what someone actually did.
Internalists say reasons must have an important connection to motivation, such as a desire or the ability to become motivated.
Externalists say some reasons may exist even when a person does not currently want the action.
There are many kinds of internalism, so the debate is not just one simple yes-or-no question.
A major challenge for some internalist views is explaining reasons that seem to apply to everyone, such as reasons not to do serious wrongs.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate helps us think carefully about advice, responsibility, and choice. If reasons always depend on what people want, then people’s different desires may give them different reasons. If some reasons are independent of desire, then a person may have a reason even when that reason has little motivational pull. Understanding the difference also helps us avoid confusing what explains an action with what justifies it.

important_terms.definition: A fact or consideration that counts in favor of or against doing something.
A reason that helps explain why someone actually did something.
The view that every reason for action must connect in some way with a person’s motivation or motivational attitudes.
The view that at least some reasons for action do not depend on the person’s motivation or desires in the way internalism claims.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be a reason for you even if you do not know about it yet?
Must you want something before you have a reason to do it?
Could a person have a reason that they strongly refuse to follow?
Why might philosophers disagree about what counts as a real reason?

summaries.example: Suppose a student will travel abroad in six months and will regret not learning the local language, although she currently feels no concern about that future regret. An externalist may say she already has a reason to study. An actual-state internalist may say that a reason must depend on some motivational state she has now. A counterfactual internalist might instead ask whether she would want to study under conditions such as full information, careful reflection, or ideal rationality. The example shows why the exact version of internalism matters.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether normative reasons for action are necessarily connected with motivation. It first distinguishes normative reasons, which justify or count for an action, from motivating reasons, which explain why an agent acted. Reasons internalism is not one single doctrine: it is a schema in which every reason must bear some relation to a motivational fact. The motivational fact may concern what the agent can be moved to do, or it may concern a psychological state such as a desire. The relation may be actual or counterfactual. The Humean Theory of Reasons is an important actual-state version, holding that a reason exists only when the agent has a desire that the action would serve. This view faces the Central Problem. Moral rationalism links wrongness with having a reason not to act, while moral absolutism says some actions are wrong regardless of an agent’s desires. If reasons depend on desires, these commitments seem to conflict. Externalists use such cases, along with prudential examples, to argue that some reasons are independent of motivation. Internalists reply in several ways: they may reject the intuitions, explain apparent external reasons as rhetorical or context-dependent, or develop a theory in which universal reasons arise from every possible motivational set. The entry concludes that the debate remains unresolved and that both sides face substantial explanatory challenges.
key_ideas: Internalism is a family of theories, formed by giving different answers about the required motivational relation and the relevant motivational fact.
Motivation views focus on what an agent is or could be moved to do; State views focus on psychological states such as desires, emotions, intentions, or aversions.
Actual versions require an actual motivational condition, while counterfactual versions appeal to what would happen under conditions such as full information or sound deliberation.
The Humean Theory of Reasons is a particularly strong actual-state view: a reason must arise from a desire that the action would serve.

The Central Problem challenges actual-state theories: if moral wrongness entails reasons, but reasons depend on desires, morality appears to vary with desires in a way that seems inconsistent with moral absolutism.

Arguments for externalism appeal to apparently universal moral or prudential reasons; arguments for internalism appeal to the agent-relative character of many ordinary reasons and to the explanatory role of motivation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue affects how we understand practical rationality, moral judgment, advice, and responsibility. It asks whether reasons have authority only when they connect with an agent’s motivational psychology or whether they can apply independently of what the agent wants. It also clarifies why philosophical arguments can pass each other: one theorist may be discussing what explains action, while another is discussing what justifies action. The many versions of internalism show that evaluating the debate requires examining the precise relation proposed between reasons, motivation, and idealized reflection.

important_terms.definition: A consideration that counts in favor of or against an action; in this entry, “reason” means a normative reason.
A psychological reason offered in answer to why someone acted; it helps explain an actual action rather than necessarily justifying it.
A thesis that every normative reason must bear some specified relation to an agent’s motivation or motivational state.
A position rejecting the claim that all normative reasons depend on motivation in the way required by internalism.
An internalist view requiring an actual desire or other motivational state that would be served by the action.
An internalist view requiring what an agent would be motivated to do, or would desire, under specified conditions.
The Humean claim that having a reason requires having a desire that the action would serve, with that desire explaining the reason.
The tension that arises when reasons depend on actual psychology but some moral reasons seem to apply regardless of an agent’s desires.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that an action would prevent your future regret give you a reason now, even if you currently lack that concern?
Can a reason exist without being capable of motivating the person who has it?
Would full information or ideal reasoning remove the dependence of reasons on a person’s actual desires?
Does blame require that someone had a reason and could have acted on it?
Are reasons for belief and reasons for action similar enough that they should receive the same theory?

summaries.example: Maya is deciding whether to practice a language for a trip next year. She does not care much about the trip yet, but she might regret being unable to communicate once she arrives. One philosopher might say Maya already has a reason to practice because the future problem counts against doing nothing. Another might say she has a reason only if some desire or concern of hers would be helped by practicing. A third might ask what Maya would want if she had complete information and thought carefully. These are different ways to approach the internal-versus-external debate.
summaries.summary: The entry studies a disagreement about the connection between reasons for action and motivation. A normative reason is something that counts in favor of or against doing something. A motivating reason is instead part of the explanation of why someone acted. Internalism says that every normative reason must be related to an agent’s motivation or motivational psychology. Externalism denies that this connection is required for every reason. Internalism comes in varieties. A Motivation view refers to what the agent is or could be moved to do. A State view refers to a psychological state, often a desire but possibly an emotion, intention, or aversion. An Actual version requires the state or motivation to be present now. A Counterfactual version asks what would happen if the agent had full information, reasoned carefully, or met another specified condition. The Humean Theory of Reasons is an influential actual-state version: a reason must be grounded in a desire that the action would satisfy. This creates the Central Problem. If moral wrongness always gives a person a reason not to act, but reasons depend on that person’s desires, then moral standards seem to depend on individual psychology. Yet some actions appear wrong regardless of what anyone wants. Externalists use this challenge, as well as examples involving long-term interests, to defend reasons that are not motivationally dependent. Internalists question whether ordinary talk really commits us to such reasons or propose ways to explain it. The source presents arguments on both sides rather than settling the issue.
key_ideas: The debate concerns normative reasons, not simply the psychological reasons that explain completed actions.
Internalism and externalism each include several different theories, because philosophers disagree about what kind of motivational connection matters.
Some internalists focus on actual desires or other states; others focus on what a person would want after gaining information or reasoning well.
The Humean Theory of Reasons says that a person has a reason only when some desire of that person would be served by the action.
A central objection is that some moral and practical reasons seem to apply even to people whose desires do not support them.
Externalists face a different concern: if reasons do not depend on motivation, it may be harder to explain why some reasons have authority for particular agents.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question matters whenever we ask what someone ought to do, whether advice gives a person a genuine reason, or whether blame is justified. It also teaches an important philosophical lesson: a theory can be challenged either by its explanation of reasons or by the particular conclusions it gives in examples. Internalism may explain why many reasons differ between people, while externalism may better fit the thought that some moral or long-term reasons apply even when motivation is absent. Careful distinctions are needed before deciding which view is stronger.

important_terms.definition: A fact that supports or counts against choosing an action.
The consideration that answers why a person performed an action.
The view that reasons must be connected to an agent’s motivation or to a motivational attitude such as a desire.
The view that some reasons can apply without the motivational connection required by internalism.
An internalist theory based on what an agent is, or could be, moved to do.
An internalist theory based on an agent’s psychological condition, such as having a desire or emotion.
A theory that requires the relevant motivational connection to exist now.
A theory that looks at what an agent would want or be motivated to do under special conditions.

questions_to_think_about: Is a reason something that must be able to motivate you, or can it exist even when you cannot see its force?
Why might a philosopher distinguish having a desire from being able to become motivated after learning more?
Does a person’s lack of concern about the future show that future-related reasons do not exist?
Can a theory allow some desire-based reasons without saying that every reason comes from desire?
What would count as a fair reason for blaming someone for an action?
